section: 2 Executing Julia programs: the Julia runtime, REPL, and program files
text:
2 Executing Julia programs: the Julia runtime, REPL, and program files

Proficiencies

Starting Julia from a shell.
Distinguishing shell commands from Julia expressions.
Using the Julia read-eval-print loop (REPL) for interactive work.
Running a Julia source file as a program.
Understanding what a .jl file is.
Understanding what println does in a script.
Passing command-line arguments to a Julia program.
Reading command-line arguments with ARGS.
Understanding the role of PROGRAM_FILE.
Using include to evaluate one Julia file from another Julia session or file.
Using @main or main(ARGS) to define a script entry point.
Running Julia with a project environment using --project.
Choosing between REPL execution and fresh-process execution in VS Code.



Executing a Julia program means starting a Julia process and asking it to evaluate Julia code. That code may come from the keyboard, from a file, from a short expression passed on the command line, or from a file that another Julia file includes. The syntax and experience differ across these cases, but the same Julia language is being evaluated.
We typically use a a shell command to invoke the Julia program to evaluate Julia code or expressions, either typed directly or sourced from a file.

A shell command is typed at the operating-system command prompt.
A Julia expression is typed at the julia> prompt or written inside a .jl file.

For example, this is a shell command to have Julia execute the contents of the file hello.jl:
$ julia hello.jl
This is Julia code:
println("Hello from Julia.")
This distinction removes many early confusions. The command julia hello.jl starts Julia. The expression println("Hello from Julia.") is code that Julia evaluates.






NotePrompt markers are not part of the command



In examples, $, julia>, pkg>, help?>, and shell> identify where text is typed. Type julia hello.jl, not $ julia hello.jl. Type println("Hello from Julia."), not julia> println("Hello from Julia.").










Concept
Meaning
Example




Shell
The program where operating-system commands are typed.
bash, zsh, PowerShell, or the VS Code integrated terminal.


Julia executable
The program named julia that starts the Julia runtime.
julia --version


Julia process
One running instance of Julia.
A REPL session or one run of julia hello.jl.


Source file
A text file containing Julia code.
hello.jl


Working directory
The directory Julia uses as the starting point for relative paths.
The result of pwd() inside Julia.



When the shell receives this command,
$ julia hello.jl
the operating system starts the julia executable. Julia initializes a new process, reads the file hello.jl, evaluates the expressions in that file, prints whatever the program explicitly prints, and then exits.
When the shell receives this command,
$ julia
the operating system starts the same julia executable, but Julia enters an interactive session instead of reading a program file. That interactive session is the REPL.

2.1 The Julia runtime
The Julia runtime is the running Julia system. It includes the language evaluator, compiler, standard library, package-loading machinery, memory management, and the process that executes the code. For beginner purposes, the runtime is what starts when the julia command works.
The simplest runtime check is:
$ julia --version
julia version 1.12.6
The exact version number may differ on another machine. The useful point is that the shell found a program named julia, started it, and Julia printed version information.
The common execution forms are:
$ julia
$ julia hello.jl
$ julia -e 'println(2 + 2)'
$ julia --project=. analysis.jl
Each form starts Julia, but each form gives Julia a different job.







Command
What Julia does




julia
Start an interactive REPL.


julia hello.jl
Evaluate the file hello.jl, then exit.


julia -e 'println(2 + 2)'
Evaluate the expression provided on the command line, then exit.


julia --project=. analysis.jl
Activate the project in the current directory, evaluate analysis.jl, then exit.



The runtime also has startup options. The options that beginners most often see are:







Option
Meaning




--version
Print the installed Julia version.


--help
Print command-line help.


--project=.
Use the current directory as the active Julia project.


--project=@.
Search upward from the current directory for a Julia project.


-e 'expression'
Evaluate a short Julia expression.


-i
Remain interactive after evaluating a file or expression.



The --project option matters once a program uses external packages. For a small file that only uses Julia’s standard functionality, julia hello.jl is enough. For a course exercise or research project with a Project.toml, use the project environment explicitly:
$ julia --project=. analysis.jl
This tells Julia which package environment to use before it evaluates the program.


2.2 The Julia REPL
REPL stands for read-eval-print loop. The REPL reads an expression, evaluates it, prints the result, and then loops back for the next expression. It is Julia’s interactive workbench.
Start it from a shell:
$ julia
Julia prints a banner and gives a prompt:
julia>
At that prompt, type Julia expressions:
julia> 2 + 3
5

julia> sqrt(16)
4.0
The REPL is useful for small experiments. It is also useful for learning because feedback is immediate. If an expression is complete, Julia evaluates it as soon as Enter is pressed. If an expression is incomplete, Julia waits for more input:
julia> function double(x)
           return 2x
       end
double (generic function with 1 method)

julia> double(10)
20
The REPL prints returned values. A script does not automatically print returned values. This is an important difference.
Consider this file:
# quiet.jl
2 + 2
Running it as a script produces no visible output:
$ julia quiet.jl
The expression was evaluated, but nothing printed it. For visible output in a script, call println, print, show, display, or another output function:
# visible.jl
println(2 + 2)
Now the script prints:
$ julia visible.jl
4
The REPL stores the value of the most recent expression in ans:
julia> 40 + 2
42

julia> ans * 10
420
Use ans only for quick interactive work. Program files should use named variables instead.

2.2.1 REPL modes
The Julia REPL has several modes. The prompt changes to show the current mode.









Mode
How to enter
Prompt
Purpose




Julia mode
Default mode
julia>
Evaluate Julia expressions.


Help mode
Type ? at an empty prompt
help?>
Search documentation.


Package mode
Type ] at an empty prompt
pkg>
Manage packages and environments.


Shell mode
Type ; at an empty prompt
shell>
Run shell commands from inside Julia.



Press Backspace at an empty mode prompt to return to Julia mode.
Help mode is especially valuable for beginners:
julia> ?
help?> println
Package mode is used later when adding and managing packages:
julia> ]
pkg> status
Shell mode is useful for quick directory checks:
julia> ;
shell> pwd
The shell mode is still shell syntax, not Julia syntax. The prompt helps keep the two languages separate.


2.2.2 The REPL working directory
The REPL has a working directory. Julia uses this directory as the starting point for relative file paths.
Check it with:
julia> pwd()
"/home/student/julia-practice"
Change it with:
julia> cd("projects")
List files with:
julia> readdir()
The shell has a working directory too. When Julia starts from a shell, Julia usually inherits the shell’s working directory. This means the following 2 workflows usually begin in the same directory:
$ pwd
/home/student/julia-practice
$ julia
julia> pwd()
"/home/student/julia-practice"
When a file cannot be found, check the working directory first.


2.2.3 Exiting the REPL
Exit the REPL with either:
julia> exit()
or press Ctrl-D at an empty julia> prompt.
Use Ctrl-C to interrupt code that is currently running. Use Ctrl-D to end the REPL session.



2.3 Julia program files
A Julia program file is a plain-text file containing Julia code. By convention, Julia source files end in .jl.
Examples:
hello.jl
analysis.jl
simulate_population.jl
plot_results.jl
The file extension does not make the code special by itself. It tells people and tools that the file contains Julia source code. When the command julia hello.jl runs, Julia reads and evaluates the file.

2.3.1 A first script
Create a file named hello.jl:
message = "Hello from a Julia file."
println(message)
Run it from the shell:
$ julia hello.jl
Hello from a Julia file.
The program has 2 expressions. The first expression creates a variable named message. The second expression prints the value stored in message.
Julia evaluates a script from top to bottom. Later expressions can use names created by earlier expressions:
radius = 3.0
area = pi * radius^2

println("radius = ", radius)
println("area = ", area)
Save that as circle_area.jl and run it:
$ julia circle_area.jl
radius = 3.0
area = 28.274333882308138
This is already a complete program. It receives no user input and uses no packages, but it executes reproducibly from a file.


2.3.2 Script output
Output is explicit. The expression area = pi * radius^2 computes and stores a value, but it does not print anything. The function println writes text to standard output, which is usually the terminal.
Use println when each output should end with a newline:
println("first line")
println("second line")
Use print when output should not automatically end with a newline:
print("radius = ")
println(radius)
For beginner scripts, println is usually the right output function.


2.3.3 Running a file by path
The file does not have to be in the current directory if the shell command gives a path to it:
$ julia scripts/hello.jl
That command asks Julia to evaluate the file hello.jl inside the scripts directory.
Relative paths start from the current working directory:
$ julia scripts/hello.jl
Absolute paths start from the root of the file system:
$ julia /home/student/julia-practice/scripts/hello.jl
Relative paths are shorter. Absolute paths are less sensitive to the current working directory.


2.3.4 The script file and the working directory
A beginner script often needs to read a data file. This is where a subtle distinction matters.
The script file has a location:
/home/student/project/scripts/analyze.jl
The Julia process also has a working directory:
/home/student/project
These are related, but they are not the same concept. When code reads a relative path such as "data/observations.csv", Julia resolves that path relative to the process working directory.
For project scripts, it is often more stable to build paths relative to the script file:
script_dir = @__DIR__
data_path = joinpath(script_dir, "..", "data", "observations.csv")
@__DIR__ expands to the directory that contains the current source file. joinpath builds a path using the conventions of the operating system. This avoids hard-coding path separators such as / or \.


2.3.5 Command-line arguments
Programs often need input from the command line. In Julia, command-line arguments passed to a script are available in the global constant ARGS.
Create show_args.jl:
println("PROGRAM_FILE = ", PROGRAM_FILE)
println("ARGS = ", ARGS)
Run it with extra words after the script name:
$ julia show_args.jl oak maple pine
PROGRAM_FILE = show_args.jl
ARGS = ["oak", "maple", "pine"]
PROGRAM_FILE stores the script file name or path. ARGS stores the arguments that came after the script name. The values in ARGS are strings.
This matters when the program expects a number:
radius_text = ARGS[1]
radius = parse(Float64, radius_text)

println(pi * radius^2)
Run it with:
$ julia circle_from_args.jl 3.0
28.274333882308138
The argument 3.0 begins as the string "3.0". The function parse(Float64, radius_text) converts that string to a Float64.


2.3.6 Julia options and program arguments
Julia command-line options come before the program file. Program arguments come after the program file.
$ julia --project=. circle_from_args.jl 3.0
In that command:

--project=. is an option for Julia.
circle_from_args.jl is the program file.
3.0 is an argument for the program.

Use -- when it helps separate Julia options from the program file and program arguments:
$ julia --project=. -- circle_from_args.jl 3.0
The delimiter is especially useful when a program argument itself starts with -:
$ julia --project=. -- report.jl --format=csv
In that command, --format=csv belongs to report.jl, not to Julia.


2.3.7 A script with functions
Short scripts can be written as top-level expressions. As soon as a script contains reusable logic, put that logic into functions.
This script separates calculation, formatting, and command-line execution:
function parse_radius(text::AbstractString)::Float64
    radius = parse(Float64, text)
    radius >= 0 || throw(ArgumentError("Expected a non-negative radius. Received $(radius)."))
    return radius
end

function circle_area(radius::Real)::Float64
    return pi * Float64(radius)^2
end

function circle_report(radius::Real)::String
    area = circle_area(radius)
    return "A circle with radius $(radius) has area $(area)."
end

radius = parse_radius(ARGS[1])
println(circle_report(radius))
Save it as circle_report.jl and run:
$ julia circle_report.jl 3.0
A circle with radius 3.0 has area 28.274333882308138.
This style is easier to test and revise than a long file of top-level statements. The functions perform the reusable work. The final lines connect those functions to command-line execution.


2.3.8 A script entry point with main
The previous script still has executable top-level code at the bottom. For larger scripts, define a main function and make the bottom of the file a small entry point.
function parse_radius(text::AbstractString)::Float64
    radius = parse(Float64, text)
    radius >= 0 || throw(ArgumentError("Expected a non-negative radius. Received $(radius)."))
    return radius
end

function circle_area(radius::Real)::Float64
    return pi * Float64(radius)^2
end

function circle_report(radius::Real)::String
    area = circle_area(radius)
    return "A circle with radius $(radius) has area $(area)."
end

function main(args::AbstractVector{<:AbstractString})::Int
    length(args) == 1 || throw(ArgumentError("Usage: julia circle_main.jl RADIUS"))

    radius = parse_radius(only(args))
    println(circle_report(radius))

    return 0
end

exit(main(ARGS))
Save it as circle_main.jl. Run it the same way:
$ julia circle_main.jl 3.0
A circle with radius 3.0 has area 28.274333882308138.
The function main receives ARGS. It returns an integer exit code. By convention, exit code 0 means success. A nonzero exit code means failure.
The line exit(main(ARGS)) is the explicit script entry point. It says: run main with the command-line arguments, then use the returned integer as the process exit code.


2.3.9 A script entry point with @main
Julia 1.11 added @main as an opt-in entry-point mechanism for scripts. On Julia 1.11 or newer, the previous script can end by defining (@main)(args):
function parse_radius(text::AbstractString)::Float64
    radius = parse(Float64, text)
    radius >= 0 || throw(ArgumentError("Expected a non-negative radius. Received $(radius)."))
    return radius
end

function circle_area(radius::Real)::Float64
    return pi * Float64(radius)^2
end

function circle_report(radius::Real)::String
    area = circle_area(radius)
    return "A circle with radius $(radius) has area $(area)."
end

function (@main)(args::AbstractVector{<:AbstractString})::Int
    length(args) == 1 || throw(ArgumentError("Usage: julia circle_main.jl RADIUS"))

    radius = parse_radius(only(args))
    println(circle_report(radius))

    return 0
end
Run it as a script:
$ julia circle_main.jl 3.0
A circle with radius 3.0 has area 28.274333882308138.
The @main form tells Julia to call Main.main(ARGS) after the script finishes loading. This makes the script entry point explicit while keeping the file clean.
For Julia versions older than 1.11, use the explicit exit(main(ARGS)) form.


2.3.10 Top-level code and reusable code
A useful beginner rule is:

Use top-level code for small experiments and short throwaway scripts.
Use functions for calculations that have names, inputs, and outputs.
Use main(args) when a file is intended to be run as a command-line program.
Keep file reading, printing, and command-line parsing near the entry point.
Keep scientific calculations in functions that receive inputs and return values.

This separation makes the program easier to test. For example, circle_area(3.0) can be tested directly in the REPL. The script entry point can remain responsible for reading ARGS and printing results.


2.3.11 Evaluating a file with include
Running a file from the shell starts a fresh Julia process:
$ julia circle_main.jl 3.0
Evaluating a file with include happens inside an existing Julia process:
julia> include("circle_report.jl")
This distinction matters. When a file is run from the shell, Julia starts clean, evaluates the file, and exits. When a file is included in the REPL, definitions remain available afterward:
julia> include("geometry.jl")
circle_report (generic function with 1 method)

julia> circle_report(3.0)
"A circle with radius 3.0 has area 28.274333882308138."
include is also how one Julia file can evaluate another Julia file.
Create geometry.jl:
function circle_area(radius::Real)::Float64
    return pi * Float64(radius)^2
end

function circle_report(radius::Real)::String
    area = circle_area(radius)
    return "A circle with radius $(radius) has area $(area)."
end
Create run_geometry.jl in the same directory:
include("geometry.jl")

println(circle_report(3.0))
Run:
$ julia run_geometry.jl
A circle with radius 3.0 has area 28.274333882308138.
The call include("geometry.jl") evaluates the contents of geometry.jl. After that, run_geometry.jl can call circle_report.
include is simple and direct. It is appropriate for splitting one program across a few files. Packages use a more formal version of this idea, organized around modules and project environments.


2.3.12 include and repeated evaluation
Calling include("geometry.jl") more than once evaluates the file more than once. This is useful during learning:
julia> include("geometry.jl")

julia> circle_area(3.0)
28.274333882308138
Edit the file, save it, and include it again:
julia> include("geometry.jl")
The REPL now has the new definitions. This workflow is convenient, but remember that the REPL session keeps old variables and loaded packages until it exits. When behavior seems confusing, restart Julia or run the script in a fresh process.


2.3.13 include, using, and import
Julia has 2 broad ways to load code:








Mechanism
Example
Purpose




Code inclusion
include("geometry.jl")
Evaluate another source file as part of the current program.


Package loading
using Statistics or import Statistics
Load a package or standard library available in the active environment.



Use include for files that are part of the same program. Use using or import for packages.
For example:
using Statistics: mean

values = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
println(mean(values))
Statistics is a standard library. The statement using Statistics: mean makes the function mean available in the program.
For external packages, Julia must find the package in the active environment. That is why project activation matters:
$ julia --project=. analysis.jl
The next lesson introduces environments, packages, and projects in more detail.


2.3.14 A beginner execution checklist
When a Julia program does not run as expected, inspect these points in order:

Confirm that the shell can find Julia.
$ julia --version
Confirm that the shell is in the intended directory.
$ pwd
$ ls
Confirm that the program file exists at the path passed to Julia.
$ julia scripts/hello.jl
Confirm that the program prints output explicitly.
println("The program reached this line.")
Confirm that command-line arguments are present before indexing ARGS.
length(ARGS) == 1 || throw(ArgumentError("Usage: julia script.jl VALUE"))
Confirm that the correct project environment is active when packages are used.
$ julia --project=. analysis.jl
Restart Julia or run in a fresh process if REPL state may be interfering.
$ julia analysis.jl



2.3.15 Common error messages








Symptom
Likely cause
First check




julia: command not found
Julia is not installed or not on the shell PATH.
Run julia --version; revisit installation.


SystemError: opening file ... No such file or directory
The file path is wrong relative to the working directory.
Check pwd() in Julia or pwd in the shell.


BoundsError involving ARGS[1]
The script expected an argument but none was supplied.
Run julia script.jl value.


ArgumentError from parse
A command-line argument could not be converted to the requested type.
Print ARGS and inspect the actual strings.


UndefVarError
A name was used before it was defined or loaded.
Check spelling, evaluation order, and include calls.


ArgumentError: Package ... not found
The package is not available in the active environment.
Start Julia with --project=. or activate the right environment.


A changed file seems ignored
The current REPL process still has older state or the edited file was not included again.
Re-run include, restart the REPL, or run a fresh process.



Errors are information. Read the first line to identify the error type, then read the stack trace from the topmost line that points into the file being edited.

text:
3 The VS Code development environment

3.1 Writing Julia programs
VS Code is an editor and development environment. It is not Julia itself. The Julia extension connects VS Code to a Julia installation and provides editor features such as syntax highlighting, code execution commands, an integrated REPL, inline results, plots, documentation lookup, and environment selection.
The usual beginner setup has 3 pieces:

Julia is installed.
VS Code is installed.
The Julia VS Code extension is installed.

Open the course or project folder in VS Code before writing code. This gives VS Code a workspace folder. The workspace folder usually becomes the working directory for integrated Julia workflows.
Create Julia files with the .jl extension:
hello.jl
circle_report.jl
analysis.jl
A good beginner habit is to keep one clear entry-point file for each exercise. For example:
exercise-01/
  Project.toml
  hello.jl
or:
population-model/
  Project.toml
  src/
    model.jl
  scripts/
    run_model.jl
For small exercises, one .jl file is enough. For larger projects, place reusable calculations in separate files and keep the script entry point small.


3.2 Executing Julia code and programs
VS Code offers more than one execution path. The difference between them is not cosmetic. They create different execution conditions.








VS Code action
Execution condition
Use when




Execute code in REPL
Sends selected code or the current top-level block to the integrated Julia REPL.
Experimenting with a function or expression.


Execute file in REPL
Evaluates the active file inside the integrated Julia REPL.
Iterating quickly while keeping a session open.


Run file in new process
Starts a new Julia process and runs the active file.
Checking that a script works from a clean start.


Start without debugging
Starts a new Julia process according to the launch configuration.
Running a configured entry-point script with chosen arguments, working directory, and environment.



The integrated REPL is persistent. Values and definitions remain until the REPL exits. This is useful while exploring, but it can hide missing code or stale state.
A fresh process is stricter. It starts Julia from scratch, evaluates the file, and exits. If the file only works in the REPL but fails in a fresh process, the file probably depends on something that was created interactively but not written into the program.
For serious checks, run the file in a fresh process. For exploration, use the REPL.

3.2.1 The command palette
Most Julia extension commands are available from the VS Code command palette:
Ctrl-Shift-P
or on macOS:
Cmd-Shift-P
Search for commands beginning with Julia:. Important beginner commands include:

Julia: Start REPL
Julia: Execute Code in REPL
Julia: Execute File in REPL
Julia: Run File in New Process
Julia: Change Current Environment

Keyboard shortcuts can differ by platform and configuration. The command palette is the reliable way to find the command by name.



3.3 Running Julia code and programs in the integrated terminal
The VS Code integrated terminal is a shell inside the editor. Commands typed there are shell commands. This is often the clearest way to learn execution because it exposes the same command-line behavior used outside VS Code.
Open the integrated terminal and run:
$ julia --version
Run a file:
$ julia hello.jl
Run a file with a project environment:
$ julia --project=. analysis.jl
Run a file with arguments:
$ julia circle_main.jl 3.0
Start the REPL in the integrated terminal:
$ julia
Then evaluate a file from the REPL:
julia> include("hello.jl")
The integrated terminal is useful because the command is visible and repeatable. If a VS Code button behaves unexpectedly, run the corresponding shell command directly.


3.4 A recommended beginner workflow
Use this workflow until the execution model feels natural.

Open the project folder in VS Code.
Open the integrated terminal.
Run julia --version to confirm that Julia is available.
Create a small .jl file.
Run it with julia file_name.jl.
If the file uses packages, run it with julia --project=. file_name.jl.
Use the REPL for experiments.
Move working ideas from the REPL into the .jl file.
Run the .jl file in a fresh process before considering it finished.

This workflow keeps exploration and reproducibility connected. The REPL supports discovery. The program file records the result. The fresh-process run proves that the file contains everything needed to execute.


3.5 Practice exercises

Exercise 3
Create a file named hello.jl. Make it print 3 lines:

your name
today’s date
the result of 2 + 2

Run it from the shell with:
$ julia hello.jl



Exercise 4Create a file named inspect_execution.jl with this content:
println("pwd() = ", pwd())
println("PROGRAM_FILE = ", PROGRAM_FILE)
println("ARGS = ", ARGS)
Run it several ways:
$ julia inspect_execution.jl
$ julia inspect_execution.jl alpha beta
$ julia --project=. inspect_execution.jl alpha beta
Describe what changes and what stays the same.



Exercise 5Create a file named rectangle_area.jl. The program should accept 2 command-line arguments, width and height, parse both as Float64, calculate the area, and print a sentence reporting the result.
Example run:
$ julia rectangle_area.jl 4.0 2.5
A rectangle with width 4.0 and height 2.5 has area 10.0.
Use functions for parsing, calculation, and reporting. Use either exit(main(ARGS)) or @main as the entry point.




3.6 Further reading

Julia command-line interface
The Julia REPL
Julia code loading
Julia modules
Running Julia code in VS Code

text:
4 Working with Julia: environments, projects, and package management

Proficiencies

Explaining what a Julia package is.
Explaining what a Julia environment is, and what Project.toml and Manifest.toml each record.
Identifying which environment is active in a Julia session, from the pkg> prompt or with Pkg.status().
Installing packages into the default global environment with Pkg.add.
Creating and activating a project-specific environment with Pkg.activate.
Explaining why Manifest.toml, not Project.toml, is what makes an environment reproducible.
Reproducing a project’s exact package versions elsewhere with Pkg.instantiate.
Choosing between a global-environment workflow and a project-based workflow for a given task, and explaining why.



Every Julia session loads packages from somewhere. That “somewhere” is called an environment, and every Julia session has one active, whether or not it is ever mentioned explicitly. What follows first explains what an environment is — this part is identical no matter how it is used — and then compares 2 common ways of using that same mechanism: a single shared environment, and a dedicated environment per project.

4.1 What a package is
A Julia package is a body of Julia code, distributed with a name and a version, that can be loaded with using or import. DataFrames, CSV, and CairoMakie are packages. Julia also ships with standard-library packages, such as Statistics and Random, that are always available without an installation step. External packages are not automatically available; they must be installed into an environment first.


4.2 What an environment is
A Julia environment is a set of packages, at specific versions, that a Julia session can load. Concretely, an environment is a pair of files:







File
Records




Project.toml
The packages an environment directly depends on, and any version constraints on them.


Manifest.toml
The complete, resolved set of packages needed to satisfy those dependencies — direct and indirect — each pinned to one exact installed version.



Project.toml is written and read by both people and Pkg. Manifest.toml is generated by Pkg and is not meant to be hand-edited.







NoteManifest.toml is machine-generated



Every Manifest.toml begins with the line # This file is machine-generated - editing it directly is not advised. Treat it as an output to inspect, not as a file to compose by hand.

At any moment, exactly one environment is the active project. Pkg.add, Pkg.status, and plain using/import all act on whichever environment is currently active. Nothing about this mechanism differs between “the global environment” and “a project environment” — a global environment is simply the environment that happens to be active by default.

4.2.1 The default global environment
Start Julia with no options, and the active project is a global environment tied to the installed Julia version:
julia> Base.active_project()
"/home/student/.julia/environments/v1.12/Project.toml"
This environment lives inside the Julia depot (~/.julia by default) and is shared by every Julia session started without --project. It is created automatically the first time it is needed and persists across sessions. The exact path differs by machine and Julia version.
Installing a package here needs no prior setup:
julia> using Pkg

julia> Pkg.add("DataFrames")
Check what is installed in the active project with Pkg.status:
julia> Pkg.status()
Status `~/.julia/environments/v1.12/Project.toml`
  [a93c6f00] DataFrames v1.8.2
The version shown will differ over time, as DataFrames releases new versions.


4.2.2 Project environments
A project environment is the same kind of Project.toml/Manifest.toml pair, kept in a project’s own directory instead of the depot. Activate one with Pkg.activate:
julia> using Pkg

julia> Pkg.activate(".")
  Activating new project at `/home/student/population-model`
Pkg.activate(".") by itself writes nothing to disk. Project.toml and Manifest.toml appear only once a package is actually added:
julia> Pkg.add("DataFrames")
   Resolving package versions...
    Updating `~/population-model/Project.toml`
  [a93c6f00] + DataFrames v1.8.2
    Updating `~/population-model/Manifest.toml`
  [a93c6f00] + DataFrames v1.8.2
  ...
From the shell, the same project can be made active for an entire run without touching code, using the --project option introduced in the previous lesson:
$ julia --project=. run_model.jl







TipReading the active environment off the pkg> prompt



The Pkg REPL-mode prompt names the active project. For the default global environment, it looks like:
(@v1.12) pkg>
For a project directory named population-model with no name field in its Project.toml, it looks like:
(population-model) pkg>
If add or status reports unexpected package versions, checking this prompt is the fastest way to confirm which environment is actually active.



4.2.3 Reproducing a project environment
Manifest.toml is what makes a project reproducible. Given both files, another machine — or the same machine after packages were never downloaded there — can recreate the identical set of package versions:
$ julia --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'
Pkg.instantiate() reads Manifest.toml and installs exactly the versions it lists. Without a Manifest.toml present, Pkg.instantiate() falls back to resolving from Project.toml alone, which can pick different versions than the ones originally used if any dependency has released a new version since. Committing both files to version control, not Project.toml alone, is what preserves reproducibility.



4.3 Two ends of one mechanism
Nothing above forces a choice between “global” and “per-project.” Both use the identical Project.toml/Manifest.toml mechanism; they differ only in where that pair lives and how many separate pairs are kept. In practice, Julia users tend toward one of 2 recognizable patterns.

4.3.1 The data-science approach: one shared environment
Install packages once, into the default global environment (or a small number of general-purpose environments), and use them across all work without activating anything project-specific.
julia> using Pkg

julia> Pkg.add(["DataFrames", "CSV", "CairoMakie"])
No --project flag, no per-analysis Project.toml. Every session starts with the same packages already available.
Why this is attractive:

There is no setup step before starting a new analysis; a package that is already installed is simply there.
It matches an interactive, exploratory workflow — a notebook, a REPL session, a quick script — where the goal is an answer, not a shareable artifact.
There is one thing to keep track of, not one thing per project.

The costs:

No reproducibility. Nothing records which package versions produced a given result. Months later, an updated package can change behavior, and there is no manifest to reconstruct the original state.
No isolation. Unrelated pieces of work share one set of installed versions. Upgrading a package for one analysis can silently change behavior in another.
Silent drift. The global environment accumulates packages over time, with no record of why any particular one is there.

When it is the right call:

Early learning, while the environment mechanism itself is not yet the point of the exercise.
Quick calculations, one-off exploration, and throwaway scripts that will not be run again or handed to anyone else.
Interactive data exploration where the analysis, not the environment, is what gets saved.



4.3.2 The developer approach: one environment per project
Give each project, package, or assignment its own directory with its own Project.toml and Manifest.toml, activated explicitly before any package is installed or used.
$ mkdir population-model && cd population-model
$ julia --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.add(["DataFrames", "CairoMakie"])'
or, from an already-running Julia session:
julia> using Pkg

julia> Pkg.activate("population-model")

julia> Pkg.add(["DataFrames", "CairoMakie"])
Every later session that needs the same packages activates the same project:
$ julia --project=. run_model.jl
Why this is worth the extra step:

Reproducibility. Manifest.toml pins exact versions. Pkg.instantiate() recreates them on another machine, or on the same machine much later.
Isolation. Adding or upgrading a package for one project cannot change behavior in another.
Shareability. Committing Project.toml and Manifest.toml alongside the code lets a collaborator, a grader, or a future reader run the same code against the same dependencies.
An explicit dependency list. Project.toml states, in one place, everything the project actually needs.

The costs:

Setup overhead: a project needs to be created and activated before it does anything useful.
More files and more state to track — remembering which project is active, and activating the right one, is a step that can be forgotten.
Forgetting to activate the intended project is a common source of confusion: code that runs against the global environment can fail once run with a --project=. that was never given the package, or the reverse.

When it is the right call:

Any code that will be handed in, published, shared, or run again after the current session ends.
Julia packages under development.
Research code, course assignments, and analyses whose exact results need to be reconstructible later.




4.4 Comparing the 2 approaches









Shared global environment
Per-project environment




Setup cost
None — packages are installed once.
One activate (and eventually instantiate) per project.


Reproducibility
None; package versions can change under a script without warning.
Exact, via Manifest.toml.


Isolation between projects
None; all work shares one set of versions.
Complete; each project has its own versions.


Shareable with a collaborator
Not directly — versions are recorded nowhere.
Yes — commit Project.toml and Manifest.toml.


Best fit
Learning, quick calculations, one-off exploration.
Assignments, packages, research code, anything reused or shared.





4.5 A practical recommendation
These are ends of a spectrum, not a binary choice, and most working practice sits somewhere in between. A reasonable path through that spectrum:

If the environment mechanism itself is not yet the point of the exercise, do not worry about it yet. The “one global environment for everything” approach is a fine place to start.
When ready to be more deliberate, keep the true default global environment clean rather than letting every package ever tried accumulate there. Create one general-purpose environment to act as a personal scratchpad/calculator for casual, everyday work, and use that instead.
Create a dedicated project environment for anything that is a package, a course assignment, or a piece of research code — anything whose results, or whose code, need to still work correctly later or on another machine.

The underlying rule is the same in every case: the less a piece of work depends on being reproduced exactly, the more acceptable a shared environment is; the more it depends on being reproduced exactly, the more a dedicated project environment earns its overhead.


4.6 Command reference








Task
Global / shared environment
Project environment




Make an environment active
Nothing to do; it is active by default.
Pkg.activate(".") or julia --project=.


Install a package
Pkg.add("PackageName")
Activate first, then Pkg.add("PackageName")


See what is installed
Pkg.status()
Pkg.status(), with the project active


Recreate the exact set of packages elsewhere
Not applicable — nothing is pinned.
Pkg.instantiate()


Share the environment with someone else
Not directly supported.
Commit Project.toml and Manifest.toml.


Remove a package
Pkg.rm("PackageName")
Activate first, then Pkg.rm("PackageName")





4.7 Common pitfalls








Symptom
Likely cause
First check




ArgumentError: Package ... not found
The package is not available in the active environment.
Check the pkg> prompt or Base.active_project() to see which environment is active.


A script works interactively but fails with julia script.jl
The REPL had a different environment active than the one the shell command used.
Re-run with the intended --project= flag explicitly.


A collaborator’s Pkg.instantiate() installs different versions
Manifest.toml was not committed, only Project.toml.
Confirm both files are tracked in version control.


Pkg.activate(".") “worked” but no Project.toml appears
Activating an empty directory writes nothing until a package is added.
Run Pkg.add for at least one package, then check again.


A once-working script now behaves differently
The global environment’s packages were updated since the script was last run, and nothing pinned their versions.
Consider moving the script into a project environment with its own Manifest.toml.





4.8 Practice exercises

Exercise 6From a fresh julia session started with no --project flag, run Base.active_project() and Pkg.status(). Note the path that is printed. Enter package mode with ] and read the prompt. Explain, in a sentence, what the text in parentheses on the pkg> prompt refers to.



Exercise 7Create a new directory named env-practice. From inside it, activate a project environment and add the Example package:
using Pkg
Pkg.activate(".")
Pkg.add("Example")
Inspect the resulting Project.toml and Manifest.toml. Identify, in Manifest.toml, the exact version of Example that was installed.



Exercise 8Delete the Manifest.toml file created in the previous exercise, keeping Project.toml. Run julia --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()' and check which version of Example is installed now. Explain why Manifest.toml, rather than Project.toml, is the file responsible for reproducibility.




4.9 Further reading

Pkg.jl: Working with Environments
Pkg.jl: Managing Packages
Pkg standard library
Julia code loading

2 Plotting geospatial data with GeoAxis

Proficiencies

Create a GeoMakie geographical figure with given vector data.









TipRecipes





Geospatial data visualization recipes



Geospatial data coordinates are encoded using a coordinate reference systems, and we need to use a special type of plotting axis, the GeoMake.GeoAxis, to convert these values to Cartesian plotting coordinates.







TipCoordinate projections



We say we are projecting the coordinates when we do this, and set of coordinates are said to be in one projection or another, depending on their particular coordinate reference systems.

The GeoMakie.jl.GeoAxis plotting axis automatically manages geospatial coordinate data projection into Cartesian coordinates. It is used with plotting functions instead of the default Cartesian coordinate system Axis when the coordinates in the data need to be projected under a particular geographic coordinate reference system or another for correct visualization or analysis.


using GeoMakie, CairoMakie
1coasts = GeoMakie.coastlines()
2fig = Figure()
3ax = GeoAxis(fig[1,1])
4lines!(ax, coasts)
5# save("coastlines.pdf", fig)
6# save("coastlines.png", fig)
7fig


1

Load coastline data into variable coasts.

2

Create a Figure object: a container for the plots.

3

Create a GeoAxis object: a geospatial CRS-equipped coordinate plotting axis.

4

Plot predefined line data on the given plotting axis.

5

Save to PDF file.

6

Save to PNG file.

7

Display in the REPL

title: Basics of geospatial coordinate reference systems
text:
3 Specifying source and destination projections

Proficiencies

Create a GeoMakie geographical figure with a background of supplied coastline data.
Using PROJ-strings to specify source and destination projections of the data.



The GeoMakie.GeoAxis function that creates and returns a GeoAxis plotting axis allows us to specify both the source data as well the destination coordinate reference systems, along with additional modifiers, using the keyword arguments source and dest, respectively. This allow us to not just to view data in its correct coordinate reference framework, but also transform or reproject the data into arbitrary projections or views. The coordinate reference systems are specified passing special String values called proj-strings (short for “project strings”). By default, GeoMakie.GeoAxis assumes that the source data are longitude and latitude decimal degrees in reference to the WGS84 datum (representation of the Earth’s shape). This corresponds to setting the source proj-string to “+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84”. By default, GeoMakie.GeoAxis also assumes that we want use the Mercator projection under the same datum. This, in turn, corresponds to setting the dest proj-string to “+proj=merc +datum=-WGS84”. As such, the default GeoAxis created without source or dest keyword arguments corresponds to:
using GeoMakie, CairoMakie
fig = Figure()                      
ax = GeoAxis(
  fig[1, 1],
  source = "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84",
  dest   = "+proj=merc +datum=WGS84"
)
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines())   
fig
crumbs: Basics of geospatial coordinate reference systems

title: Basics of geospatial coordinate reference systems
text:
4 Plotting alternate projections or views

Proficiencies

Specify alternative map projections using the dest keyword argument of GeoAxis.
Recognize common projection families and their trade-offs (equal-area, conformal, compromise).



The dest proj-string controls the map projection: the mathematical transformation used to flatten the curved surface of the Earth onto a two-dimensional plane. Every projection makes trade-offs, preserving some spatial properties (area, shape, distance, direction) at the cost of others. The proj-string +proj=<name> selects a named projection; additional parameters refine it.

4.1 Equirectangular (Plate Carrée) projection
The equirectangular projection maps longitude directly to the x-axis and latitude directly to the y-axis, producing the familiar rectangular grid of the standard wall map. It is the simplest possible projection and serves as a useful baseline. However, it is neither equal-area not conformal, and distortion increases severely toward the poles.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=longlat")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig






4.2 Equal Earth projection
The Equal Earth projection is an equal-area pseudocylindrical projection designed to give continents their correct relative sizes while remaining visually appealing.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig






4.3 Robinson projection
The Robinson projection is a compromise projection — it does not perfectly preserve area, shape, or distance, but minimizes overall distortion, giving a visually balanced view of the world. It was used by National Geographic for several decades.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=robin")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig






4.4 Mollweide projection
The Mollweide projection is an equal-area elliptical projection. Meridians are elliptical arcs and parallels are horizontal straight lines, with spacing increasing toward the equator to preserve area.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=moll")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig






4.5 Orthographic projection
The orthographic projection renders the Earth as it would appear from a distant point in space — a perspective view of a hemisphere. It is neither equal-area nor conformal, but is immediately intuitive.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=ortho +lat_0=20 +lon_0=15")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig




The +lat_0 and +lon_0 parameters set the latitude and longitude of the center of the visible hemisphere. Regions beyond the horizon are automatically excluded from the plot.






TipChoosing a projection








Projection
Proj-string
Preserves
Common use




Mercator
+proj=merc
Shape (conformal)
Navigation, web maps


Equal Earth
+proj=eqearth
Area
Thematic maps


Robinson
+proj=robin

title: Basics of geospatial coordinate reference systems
text:
5 Plotting alternate centers or framing

Proficiencies

Re-center a map projection on an arbitrary longitude using the +lon_0 proj-string parameter.
Recognize when re-centering is appropriate for visualizing data in a particular ocean basin or hemisphere.



Every projection has a natural central meridian, the longitude that runs vertically through the center of the map. By default this is \(0°\) (the prime meridian), which places the Pacific Ocean split between the left and right edges of the map. The +lon_0 parameter shifts the central meridian to any target longitude, rotating the entire map so that longitude appears in the center. This is useful when your data are concentrated in a region that would otherwise be split across the map edges — Pacific-basin biodiversity studies, for instance, benefit from centering near \(180°\) or \(-150°\).

5.1 Default centering: \(0°\), the prime meridian

fig = Figure()
1ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=0")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig


1

+lon_0=0 centers the projection on the prime meridian; this is the default and can be omitted.









5.2 Center on \(-100°\) (central North America)

fig = Figure()
1ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=-100")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig


1

+lon_0=-100 centers the map on \(100°\,\text{W}\), roughly the center of North America. The Pacific and Atlantic Oceans are now split at the edges.









5.3 Center on \(120°\) (eastern Asia / western Pacific)

fig = Figure()
1ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=120")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig


1

+lon_0=120 centers the map on \(120°\,\text{E}\), suitable for visualizing data across eastern Asia and the western Pacific.









5.4 Plotting across the antimeridian
Centering the map on \(180°\) (the antimeridian) or plotting data that spans it can produce rendering artifacts: line segments whose endpoints straddle the \(\pm180°\) boundary are drawn as long near-horizontal lines traversing the full width of the plot, because the renderer naively connects the two endpoints without wrapping.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=180")
1lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines())
fig


1

Passing plain GeoMakie.coastlines() without the axis argument does not clip or re-segment coastlines to the current projection, so segments that cross the antimeridian produce long horizontal streaks.









Figure 1




Passing the GeoAxis object into GeoMakie.coastlines(ax) allows GeoMakie to perform axis-aware clipping and re-segmentation of the coastline geometries, resolving most antimeridian artifacts:

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=180")
1lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig


1

Supplying the GeoAxis to coastlines enables axis-aware geometry handling; GeoMakie clips and re-segments features at the projection boundary before rendering, eliminating the crossing artifacts.









Figure 2










TipAntimeridian issues with your own data





The axis-aware GeoMakie.coastlines(ax) approach works for the built-in coastlines dataset. If you are plotting your own polygon or linestring geometries from, say, a GeoDataFrame or a NaturalEarth dataset loaded with NaturalEarth.jl, you will need to handle antimeridian splitting yourself before passing coordinates to lines! or poly!. One approach is to preprocess geometries using GeoInterface.jl-compatible tools to split any segment that crosses \(\pm180°\) into two segments terminating at the boundary:
Plotting across the antimeridian

title: Basics of geospatial coordinate reference systems
text:
6 Regional views with plot limits

Proficiencies

Use the limits keyword argument on GeoAxis to restrict the rendered region to a geographic bounding box.
Identify appropriate longitude and latitude bounds for a region of interest.



The limits keyword argument on GeoAxis accepts a four-element tuple (lon_min, lon_max, lat_min, lat_max) and clips the view to that bounding box.

6.1 Southeast Asia
Southeast Asia spans roughly 92°E to 141°E and 11°S to 28°N.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1];
    limits = (92, 141, -11, 28))
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig




We can use dest = "+proj=longlat" to specify an equirectangular projection.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1];
    dest   = "+proj=longlat",
    limits = (92, 141, -11, 28))
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig






6.2 The Americas

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(
    fig[1, 1];
    limits = (-170, -30, -60, 75),
)
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig




We can use the dest keyword to specify a transformation the projection.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(
    fig[1, 1];
    dest = "+proj=longlat",
    limits = (-170, -30, -60, 75),
)
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig






6.3 Australia
Australia spans roughly 112°E to 155°E and 45°S to 10°S.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1];
    limits = (112, 155, -45, -10))
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig




Or, using dest = "+proj=longlat" to specify an equirectangular projection.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1];
    dest   = "+proj=longlat",
    limits = (112, 155, -45, -10))
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig

title: Basics of working with data tables
text:
1 What is tabular data?
Datasets are often organized as tables: rectangular grids of values where each row represents one observation (a specimen, a time-point, a site, a sequencing read) and each column represents one variable or attribute measured for every observation (body mass, collection date, latitude, base-call quality score).







TipRows are observations; columns are variables



This convention — one row per observation, one column per variable — is called tidy data. It is the standard expected by virtually every data-analysis and plotting library you will encounter. Keeping your own data in this form from the start will save a great deal of reformatting later.

A small example of a tabular dataset:



specimen_id
species
body_mass_g
collection_year




BM_001
Peromyscus maniculatus
21.4
2019


BM_002
Peromyscus leucopus
23.1
2019


BM_003
Mus musculus
18.7
2020



Three rows, four columns. Each row is one specimen; each column is one thing we recorded about every specimen.
crumbs: Basics of working with data tables

title: Basics of working with data tables
text:
2 File formats for tabular data






NoteSample files in different formats




Comma-separated value (“CSV”) files, with extension .csv: specimens_10.csv
Tab-separated values (“TSV”) files, with extension .tsv: specimens_10.tsv
Excel files: specimens_10.xlsx



Tabular datasets are stored in a variety of file formats. The format you receive will determine which Julia function you use to load it, so it is worth being able to identify them.

2.1 CSV and its variants
The most common plain-text format for tabular data is CSV (comma-separated values). A CSV file stores the table as lines of text. The first line is typically a header listing the column names; every subsequent line is one row of data. Values within each line are separated by a delimiter — most often a comma (,), giving the format its name, though tabs (\t) and semicolons (;) are also common.







NoteInspecting a CSV file directly



Because CSV files are plain text, you can read them in any text editor or print their first few lines in the shell:
head -5 specimens.csv
or in Julia:
open("specimens.csv") do f
    for _ in 1:5
        println(readline(f))
    end
end
This is useful for confirming the delimiter, checking whether there is a header row, and spotting any obvious formatting issues before you try to parse the file.

A CSV file corresponding to the table above would look like this:
specimen_id,species,body_mass_g,collection_year
BM_001,Peromyscus maniculatus,21.4,2019
BM_002,Peromyscus leucopus,23.1,2019
BM_003,Mus musculus,18.7,2020
A TSV (tab-separated values) file is identical in structure, but with tab characters between values rather than commas:
specimen_id⟶species⟶body_mass_g⟶collection_year
BM_001⟶Peromyscus maniculatus⟶21.4⟶2019
Both extensions — .csv and .tsv — are strong signals of the format, but always confirm by opening the file.


2.2 Excel files
Excel workbooks (.xlsx, and the older .xls) store tables in a binary format: you cannot read them as plain text. They can contain multiple worksheets in a single file. When working with Excel data in Julia, you will need to specify both the file path and which worksheet you want.

section: 3 Setting up your Julia environment for tabular data
text:
3 Setting up your Julia environment for tabular data
Before we can work with tabular data, we need to install the DataFrames.jl, which gives us the DataFrame object type, In addition, we will install CSV.jl and XLSX.jl to allow us to access data stored in some common file formats. Installation is done through Julia’s built-in package manager, Pkg.
Installations can be done either globally, across your entire Julia ecosystem, or restricted to specific project environments.

3.1 Install globally
A global install makes the package available in any Julia session on your machine, regardless of which directory you are in or which project environment you have activated.
using Pkg
Pkg.add(["DataFrames", "CSV", "XLSX"])
You only need to do this once per Julia version. After installation, using DataFrames will work in any session.


3.2 Install for a project
If you are working inside a project directory — one that contains a Project.toml file — activate the project environment first, then add the packages. This records the dependency in Project.toml and pins exact versions in Manifest.toml, so anyone who clones the project gets the same package versions you used.
using Pkg
Pkg.activate(".")
Pkg.add(["DataFrames", "CSV", "XLSX"])
Once the environment is active, all subsequent Pkg operations in that session apply to the project rather than to the global environment.

title: Basics of working with data tables
text:
4 The DataFrame type
In Julia, the standard representation of a data table is a DataFrame object from the DataFrames package.
A DataFrame holds a collection of named columns, where each column is a typed Vector. This means every value in a given column must be of the same type (all integers, all floating-point numbers, all strings, and so on), but different columns can have different types — exactly as in a real dataset.
using DataFrames

4.1 Creating a DataFrame manually from column vectors
The most direct way to construct a DataFrame is to pass named column vectors to the DataFrame constructor:

using DataFrames

specimens = DataFrame(
    specimen_id      = ["BM_001", "BM_002", "BM_003"],
    species          = ["Peromyscus maniculatus", "Peromyscus leucopus", "Mus musculus"],
    body_mass_g      = [21.4, 23.1, 18.7],
    collection_year  = [2019, 2019, 2020]
)

Each keyword argument becomes a column: the argument name is the column name, and the vector on the right is the column’s data. All vectors must have the same length.







TipColumn types are inferred automatically



Julia infers the element type of each column from the vector you supply. ["BM_001", "BM_002", "BM_003"] becomes a Vector{String} column; [21.4, 23.1, 18.7] becomes a Vector{Float64} column. You can confirm the types of all columns at once with describe(df), discussed below.

title: Basics of working with data tables
text:
5 Reading tabular data from files
In practice you will almost never type your data in by hand. Most of the time you will load it from a file written by an instrument, a database export, a collaborator’s spreadsheet, or a public data repository.

5.1 Reading CSV files with CSV.jl
The CSV package provides the CSV.read function, which parses a delimited text file and, when combined with DataFrame, returns the result as a DataFrame:
using CSV, DataFrames

specimens = CSV.read("specimens.csv", DataFrame)
CSV.read takes two required arguments: the path to the file, and the sink type that determines what kind of object the parsed data is placed into. Passing DataFrame as the sink is by far the most common usage.







NoteCommon keyword arguments for CSV.read



CSV.read accepts a large number of optional keyword arguments for handling real-world files that do not follow a perfectly clean format:
# File uses semicolons as the delimiter
CSV.read("data.csv", DataFrame; delim = ';')

# File uses tabs as the delimiter
CSV.read("data.tsv", DataFrame; delim = '\t')

# Skip the first two lines (e.g., a metadata header)
CSV.read("data.csv", DataFrame; skipto = 3)

# Treat "NA" and "" as missing values
CSV.read("data.csv", DataFrame; missingstring = ["NA", ""])

# File has no header row; supply column names manually
CSV.read("data.csv", DataFrame; header = ["id", "mass", "year"])
When a file refuses to parse cleanly, these keyword arguments are the first place to look.

For a TSV file, specify the delimiter explicitly:
specimens = CSV.read("specimens.tsv", DataFrame; delim = '\t')


5.2 Reading Excel files with XLSX.jl
The XLSX package provides access to Excel workbooks. The XLSX.readtable function reads one worksheet and returns it in a form that can be passed directly to the DataFrame constructor:
using XLSX, DataFrames

specimens = DataFrame(XLSX.readtable("specimens.xlsx", "Sheet1"))
The second argument to XLSX.readtable is the name of the worksheet to read.







TipListing the worksheets in a workbook



If you do not know the names of the worksheets in an Excel file, you can inspect them:
xf = XLSX.readxlsx("specimens.xlsx")
XLSX.sheetnames(xf)
This returns a Vector{String} listing the names of all worksheets in the workbook.

text:
7 Selecting columns
Once you have a DataFrame in memory, the most fundamental operation is selecting the columns you want to work with.

7.1 Selecting a single column as a Vector
Use the . accessor or square-bracket syntax with a Symbol or String:

specimens.body_mass_g          # returns a Vector{Float64}

3-element Vector{Float64}:
 21.4
 23.1
 18.7



specimens[!, :body_mass_g]     # identical result

3-element Vector{Float64}:
 21.4
 23.1
 18.7



specimens[!, "body_mass_g"]    # also identical

3-element Vector{Float64}:
 21.4
 23.1
 18.7









Tip! vs : as the row selector



In DataFrames indexing, the first argument selects rows and the second selects columns. Using ! as the row selector means all rows, without copying — you get a direct reference to the underlying column vector. Using : also selects all rows, but returns a copy. For read-only inspection, ! is fine and slightly more efficient. When you intend to modify the values in the returned vector and do not want to affect the original DataFrame, use :.



7.2 Selecting multiple columns as a new DataFrame
Pass a Vector of column names to get a new DataFrame containing only those columns:

specimens[!, ["specimen_id", "body_mass_g"]]

8 Filtering rows
To extract the subset of rows that satisfy some condition, use boolean indexing.

8.1 Boolean indexing
Constructing a logical (boolean) condition over a column produces a Vector{Bool} — a vector of true/false values, one per row:

specimens.collection_year .== 2019

3-element BitVector:
 1
 1
 0


Passing this boolean vector as the row index returns only the rows where the condition is true:

specimens[specimens.collection_year .== 2019, :]

NoteBroadcasting with .



The . before comparison operators (.==, .>, .<=, and so on) is Julia’s broadcasting syntax. It applies the operator element-wise across the entire vector, rather than trying to compare the whole vector to a scalar at once. You will need this . prefix whenever applying a scalar comparison across a column.
# ✓ correct: element-wise comparison
specimens.body_mass_g .> 20.0

# ✗ will error: comparing a Vector to a scalar without broadcasting
specimens.body_mass_g > 20.0

Combining multiple conditions uses & (and) and | (or), with each condition wrapped in parentheses:

specimens[(specimens.body_mass_g .> 20.0) .& (specimens.collection_year .== 2019), :]

TipIn-place modification vs. returning a new DataFrame



Assignment with df.new_column = ... modifies the DataFrame in place, changing the original object. Many DataFrames functions — select, filter, transform — return a new DataFrame instead of modifying the original. This is the standard functional style and is generally preferred because it makes it easy to trace where each transformation happened. Use in-place assignment sparingly and deliberately.

The transform function is the idiomatic way to derive new columns from existing ones without modifying the original:

title: Basics of working with randomness and probabilities
text:
Proficiencies

Sampling a single random value of a specified numeric type (e.g., Int, Float64) using rand.
Sampling multiple random values of the specified type and length using rand.
Sampling uniformly from \((0, 1]\) using rand()
How to sample a vector of independent uniform random Float64 values in \((0, 1]\) by passing a length to rand.
How to sample a matrix of independent uniform random Float64 values in \((0, 1]\) by passing row and column dimensions to rand.
How to sample uniformly at random from a defined integer range using rand with a range argument (e.g., rand(-500:500, n)).
How to sample uniformly at random from an explicit collection of values (e.g., an array of floats or characters) using rand.












TipFunctions vs methods in Julia



In Julia, a function is a operation that can accept inputs and returns outputs. A function of a particular name (e.g. range, rand, my_custom_function) may have a number of different methods, or implementation that are distinguished by the pattern of arguments the function takes (called the signature of the function).
See: Julia: Functions, methods, and signatures

The rand function is the function we will most often use to generate random variates of different shapes, and sizes and characteristics. The rand function has a number of different methods, that is, different approaches for generating random values of various different data types, structures, and ranges, depending on the arguments passed to it.



The core Julia library provides rand methods that generate values by sampling them from ranges and collections under a uniform probability distribution. Packages such as Distributions.jl, covered separately, provide the ability to sample random values from a broader range of distributions.






TipProbability distributions

title: Basics of working with randomness and probabilities
section: 2 Simulating a Bernoulli trial with rand
text:
2 Simulating a Bernoulli trial with rand
We can use rand(), which returns a uniformly distributed real value in \([0, 1)\) to determine whether or not an event of given probability occurs or not in a particular sample (outcome, realization, draw, run, etc.) of a random system.
For an event with some given probability value, if the value returned by the rand() function is less than this value we consider the event to have occurred. By default then, if the result of rand() is greater than this value, the event has not occured.





Consider 1000 samples from a uniform distribution on a subset of real number line between \(0\) and \(1\).
If we consider a uniform distribution on a subset of real number line between \(0\) and \(1\), and divide it at \(p\) of various values, we can see the larger segment of the range assigned to one or the other outcome depending the parameter.
If we consider that rand() will return a sample anywhere in that range with equal probability, we can see how a larger \(p\) means a value will fall in the part of the range that maps to the first outcome and vice versa.
if the result of arand() is less than \(p\), then we have simulated a sample in which the event has occurred, and conversely, if greater than or equal to \(p\), to not have occured.
For example, consider the classical Bernoulli trial modeling an idealized fair coin toss, where there are two possible outcomes, “heads” or “tails”, with the probability of “heads” in any single realization being given by the model parameter \(p=0.5\).
The short-hand Julia expression for this is:

rand() < 0.5 ? "heads" : "tails"

"heads"


Or, for a more readable, flexible, extensible, as well as maintanable, we define a named function that takes an argument which allows us to specify the probability parameter:

function bernoulli(p::Float64)::String
    if rand() < p
        "heads"
    else
        "tails"
    end
end
bernoulli(0.5)

"tails"

title: Pseudo-random number generators: continuous values from discrete machines
text:
A computer’s RNG (Random Number Generator), generates (pseudo-)random integer values. For continous value, the computer will generate values by sampling from a grid in \([0, 1)\).
As with the challenges of a deterministic machine generating random values, when requiring random continuous value, we are faced with the challenge of a discrete-value calculating machine dealing with non-integer values. A computer can generate a pseudo-random integer value, \(k\), using its Pseudo-Random Number Generator. For continuous values, the generated integer value, \(k\) is then scaled to a floating-point \(x\) by, for e.g., \(\frac{k}{2p}\), where \(p\) is the number usable bits and \(0 \le k \le 2^p - 1\). The result in floating point value in the range \(0 \le x < 1\).
While 1 is excluded from the range, this does not change the distribution. A continuous uniform distribution on \([0, 1]\) assigns probability zero to any single point, include \(0\) or \(1\) in that range, so this exclusion of 1 does not change the characteristics of the distribution. (With continuous distributions, we do not ask what is the probability of observing any particular value. We ask is the probability of observing a range of values.)
Let

\(p\) = number of mantissa bits of the target floating-point type (\(p=53\) for Float64)
\(k\) drawn uniformly from

\[
{0,1,\dots,2^p - 1}
\]
Define
\[
x = \frac{k}{2^p}.
\]
Then:

The mapping \(k \mapsto x\) is bijective
Each possible \(x\) has probability exactly \(2^{-p}\)
The support is

\[
\left\{ 0, \frac{1}{2^p}, \frac{2}{2^p}, \dots, \frac{2^p-1}{2^p} \right\}
\subset [0,1)
\]
Note this is a discrete uniform distribution over the set of values \(\{0, \frac{1}{2^p}, \frac{2}{2^p}, \ldots, \frac{2^p-1}{2^p}\}\), not a continuous one. The operation bins the range \([0, 1)\) into \(2^p\) equal width bins of \(\frac{1}{1^p}\) width. For Float64 this result in \(2^{53} \approx 9 \times 10^{15}\) bins of width \(2^{-53} \approx 1.11 \times 10^{-16}\).

title: Virulence-transmission trade-off (Frank, 1996)
text:
The classical virulence-transmission trade-off function, following the notation of (Frank 1996), is:
\[
R_0 = \frac{\beta(\nu)N}{\delta + \nu + c(\nu)},
\]
where:

\(R_0\) The basic reproduction number. The expected number of secondary infections produced by a single infected host introduced into a fully susceptible population of size \(N\). The transmission intensity multiplied by mean infectious duration.
\(\nu\) Virulence. In this formulation, \(\nu\) is the disease-induced host mortality intensity. This represents the per-capita hazard at which infected hosts die because of the pathogen.
\(\beta(\nu)\) Transmission coefficient (often called the transmission intensity). It gives the per-capita rate at which an infected host generates new infections per susceptible host, and it is assumed to depend on virulence. The biological trade-off is encoded here: increasing \(\nu\) may increase within-host replication and hence transmission, so \(\beta'(\nu) > 0\) over some range.
\(N\) Total density (or number) of susceptible hosts in the population at invasion. Because \(R_0\) is defined at the start of an epidemic, essentially all hosts are susceptible, so the force of infection scales with \(N\).
\(\delta\) Background host mortality intensity (natural death intensity unrelated to infection). This removes infected hosts independently of the pathogen’s virulence.
\(c(\nu)\) Additional loss intensity associated with infection that is not direct mortality. Examples include recovery with immunity, behavioral isolation, treatment, or reduced contact rate induced by symptoms. It may depend on virulence if, for example, more virulent infections provoke faster immune clearance or stronger behavioral avoidance.








TipIntensity vs. rate



All intensities are rates, but not all rates are intensities. A rate is a general term indicating the change of one quantity relative to another, expresed as a ratio (“rate” and “ratio” have the same linguistic root). An “intensity” is a rate, but one some characteristics is the instantaneous hazard parameter (= rate) of a stochastic process. In classical ODE epidemic models (e.g., SIR), “rate” and “intensity” are often used interchangeably because constant hazards produce exponential waiting times and yield linear per-capita ODE terms.

Note that:
\[
R_0 = \text{transmission intensity} \times \text{mean infection duration}.
\]

The numerator, \(\beta(\nu)N\), is the transmission intensity, i.e. the per-capita intensity (or rate) of generating new infections in a population of size \(N\).
The denominator \(\delta + \nu + c(\nu)\) gives the total removal intensity of infected hosts: the rate of removal of infected hosts from the population. Thus, \(\frac{1}{\delta + \nu + c(\nu)}\) gives the mean infectious duration.

As \(R_0\) measures the net increase of infected host over time, expressed as a ratio of infected hosts gain (the numerator) to infected hosts lost (the denominator), it serves as an index of the epidemiological state of an infectious disease. - If the numerator is greater than the denominator, there will be more infections generated than removed from the population, leading to a net increase in infections: the disease in an epidemic phase. - If the numerator is less than the denominator, there infections will be removed from the population faster than new infections will occur: the disease will “die out” without becoming an epidemic.




 Back to topReferences

Frank, Steven A. 1996. “Models of Parasite Virulence.” The Quarterly Review of Biology 71 (1): 37–78. https://doi.org/10.1086/419267.

title: Pseudo-random number generators: best practices
section: 2 Explicitly set the default random number generator seed for replicability
text:
2 Explicitly set the default random number generator seed for replicability
In most cases, however, replicability is important.
As discussed in the primer on pseudo-random number generators, the random number “seed” value passed to the algorithm determines the value of every number generated from the algorithm: in a sense, it indexes or selects a specific sequence of pre-determined random outcomes to be used.
Different seed values produce different sequences of random numbers, while conversely, the same seed value repeatedly and reliabily produces the same sequence of randomness across independent runs of the program.
This latter is what gives PRNG’s their great utility in many research software applications, and is actually useful in programming and software development as well for debugging purposes: you can only reliably be sure of fixing an error if you can reliably reproduce it to be able to work on it.
You can use default random number implicitly but gain replicability by explicitly setting its seed using the Random.seed! function.
using Random

# Explicitly seed the default random number generator with 42
Random.seed!(42)

# Implict usage of global default random number generator, seed globally set previously
rand(Int, 10)
rand(['A', 'C', 'G', 'T'])
As before, when rand is called without a random number generator object as its first argument, the default random number genrator will be used as the source of randomness. However, here we have set the seed for this before hand.

title: Pseudo-random number generators: best practices
section: 3 Explicitly reference the default random number generator for maintainability and extensibility
text:
3 Explicitly reference the default random number generator for maintainability and extensibility
While implicit usage of the default random number generator is convenient, it is good practice to always be explicit about the random number generator that is being used event if it is the default.
rng = Random.default_rng()
Random.seed!(rng, 42)
rand(rng, Int, 10)
rand(rng, ['A', 'C', 'G', 'T'])
Beyond clarity, it also makes it easy to use other random number generators if the need arises.
Furthermore, when writing our own methods for rand, the general principle is that any function doing random sampling should ideally accept an rng::AbstractRNG argument with a default of Random.default_rng(), following the convention used throughout Base and most Julia packages.

title: Pseudo-random number generators: best practices
section: 4 Ensure randomness across replicates by using time and process id’s as seeds
text:
4 Ensure randomness across replicates by using time and process id’s as seeds
While replicability is important, at the same time, in almost every case except when actually wanting to reproduce a run for debugging or study purposes, when we are running programs that use these values, we want them to have different random sequences across different independent runs.
A common convention to have a new explicitly-specified random seed on every independent run without needing to change the code (or force the user to type one in) is to use the system time, specified in nanoseconds, time_ns(), (sometimes with the process id, getpid(), added to avoid correlations when executed in bulk in parallel).
using Random

rng = Random.default_rng()
seed = time_ns() + getpid()
@info "Setting random seed: $(seed)"
Random.seed!(seed)

title: Pseudo-random number generators: best practices
section: 5 Explicitly create anmd manage your own random number generators for robust reproducibility and replicability
text:
5 Explicitly create anmd manage your own random number generators for robust reproducibility and replicability
In the full and final production-grade software, you should design all your programs to (1) optionally take a user-specific random number seed and, if not given, generate your own; (2) report and log the random number seed used; and (3) instantiate and use your own random number generator object in all computation, passing it around to different functions or objects that need them.
using Random

# Instantiate a PRNG using the "Xoshiro" algorithm with the seed value of 42
rng = Random.Xoshiro(42)
# Instantiate a PRNG using the "Mersenne Twister" with the seed value of 1999
rng = Random.MersenneTwister(1999)

# Use `rand` with the `rng` to sample an `Int` (integer) value
rand(rng, Int, 10)
# Use `rand` with the `rng` to sample a random value from the list
rand(rng, ['A', 'C', 'G', 'T'])

title: Bernoulli trial
text:
A “Bernoulli trial” is a model of randomness in which there are two possible elementary outcomes in the sample space, with the probability of one outcome given by the model parameter \(p\) (and the probability of the other is then \(1-p\)).
The iconic example is that of a single toss of a coin. If the coin is fair, that is, equally likely to land with either of its two sides, typically designated “heads” or “tails”, then it can be modeled as a Bernoulli trial with parameter \(p = 0.5\) giving the probability of “heads”. Conversely, a trick coin may have the a “heads” on both sides, thus always landing with a “heads” result, an or a “tails”
